title: How do you structure a case where the client wants to grow?
description: "How can the client grow?" The client wants more revenue and is open to options.
hook: Structure a growth case by sorting every option into four buckets: sell more of today's products to today's customers, take today's products to new customers or markets, build new products for today's customers, and diversify into new products for new customers. Then size each option, check they add up to the target, and say whether to build, partner or buy.
body:
When you will use it

The client wants more revenue and is open to options: "How can we grow 25% in three years?" or "Where should our next $10M of revenue come from?"

This is a generate question: "How can we do this?" Lay out the options in buckets that do not overlap, size them, then pick the best few. More on the three families of case questions. If the client is asking whether to enter one specific market, use the market entry structure instead.

Ask this first

How much growth, by when? Which parts of the business grow today, and is anything off the table?

The target matters because it tells you how big the options must be. A 5% goal can come from pricing and retention. A 50% goal almost always needs new markets, new products or an acquisition.

The structure

  • With existing products
    • Sell more to current customers: more visits, bigger orders, better retention, price
    • Reach new customers or markets: new cities, segments, channels
  • With new products
    • For current customers: beans and pods for home, a subscription
    • For new customers (diversification): bottled coffee drinks in supermarkets

The examples are for a coffee chain. This two-by-two is known as the Ansoff matrix. Risk rises as you move away from what the client already sells to the people it already sells to, so the top-left bucket is usually the cheapest and fastest place to start. For each option you keep, say how you would get there: build, partner or buy.

A worked example: size the options and avoid double counting

An illustrative subscription company has 100,000 customers paying $20 a month. Annual revenue is 100,000 × $20 × 12 = $24M. Management wants 25% growth, which is $6M.

Break revenue into its drivers: customers × revenue per customer × 12 months. Each growth lever moves one driver:

  • New customers through marketing, partners or new segments
  • Retention: fewer cancellations
  • Price and tiers: higher revenue per customer
  • Add-ons: related products sold to the same customers

Suppose the plan assumes 15% more customers and a 10% price rise. The growth is not 15% + 10% = 25%. It is 1.15 × 1.10 − 1 = 26.5%, because the new customers also pay the higher price. Revenue would be $30.36M.

That looks like the target is met. But the two levers interact the other way too. If the price rise makes 5% of customers cancel, customers end at 100,000 × 1.15 × 0.95 = 109,250, paying $22. Revenue is 109,250 × $22 × 12 = $28.84M, growth of about 20%, short of the target by more than $1M. The lesson: size levers together, not one at a time.

Finally, rank options on profit and investment, not revenue alone. A new channel that brings in $5M of revenue at $5.5M of extra cost is not growth worth having.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I'd split the options into existing and new products, each for existing and new customers. Starting closest to home: a 10% price rise adds about $2.4M, and 15,000 new customers through partnerships add about $3.6M. Together that's the $6M we need, but the price rise could raise cancellations, so I'd test price in one region first and keep a new-product option in reserve."

A weak answer lists ten ideas, from loyalty apps to entering China, with no sizes, no order and no check that they reach the target.

Common mistakes

  • Listing ideas without sizing them. An idea without a rough number cannot be prioritised.
  • Not checking the total. Add up your top options and compare with the target.
  • Double counting. Levers interact: price affects retention, and new customers may cannibalise old ones.
  • Jumping to diversification. The riskiest bucket is rarely the place to start.
  • Only thinking about new customers. Keeping existing customers is often cheaper and bigger.

Practise it

1. A gym chain has 40 gyms, 2,500 members per gym and a price of $40 a month. It wants 20% more revenue in three years. Do these options get there: four new gyms, a $2 price rise, $3 a month of extra spend per member on training and drinks, and 5% more members from better retention?

Show the answer

Today: 40 × 2,500 = 100,000 members × $40 × 12 = $48M. Target: 20% = $9.6M (about 6.3% a year).

  • New gyms at maturity: 4 × 2,500 × $40 × 12 = $4.8M
  • Price: 100,000 × $2 × 12 = $2.4M
  • Extra spend: 100,000 × $3 × 12 = $3.6M
  • Retention: 5,000 × $40 × 12 = $2.4M

Total: $13.2M, above the target with a buffer. But new gyms take time to fill and the price rise may hurt retention, so the realistic total is lower. Start with retention: churn is usually the biggest lever in gyms.

2. How should a newspaper grow digital subscriptions?

Show the answer
  • Reach: traffic from search, social and newsletters; new audiences and topics
  • Conversion: paywall design, trials, price, sign-up friction
  • Retention: reading habits, apps, bundles, cancellation and win-back
  • Revenue per subscriber: tiers, family plans, annual against monthly billing

Start with the funnel: find the step with the biggest drop-off. The trap is listing marketing ideas without the reach, convert, retain logic.

Where to practise next
